sentences.text: The kite was good.
That was the frustrating part.
If the kite had been bad, Dai would have known what to do.
He would have taken it apart and started again and the whole thing would have been simple.
But it was good, and he knew it was good, and it still would not fly.
He had made it in April from his father's instructions, which were written on the back of an envelope in his father's small square handwriting and which had been in the kitchen drawer for six years.
The spars were bamboo out of the old window blind that had been in the shed since before they moved in.
The sail was paper the colour of weak tea, glued along the folds and then glued again where the first glue had gone brittle.
The bridle knots were the ones on the envelope, tied four times each until he got them right.
Every measurement was correct.
He had checked them against the envelope twice and against a metre rule once.
It went up eight feet and came down like a dropped coat.
It did it thirteen times.
Not a spin, not a dive — nothing dramatic enough to be interesting.
It went up, it hesitated, the nose came round, and it settled onto the grass with a small papery sound that Dai came to hate more than he had ever hated a sound.
The crows on the telephone wire watched all six.
There were seven of them.
He noticed the number on about the fourth attempt, because they were in a row and evenly spaced, which crows are not usually, and because they had not moved.
Crows on a wire shuffle.
They open a wing and shut it.
They shout at each other.
They leave and come back.
These sat.
They watched the way a builder watches somebody else's wall — not unkindly, but with a professional attention that made Dai's ears go hot.
On the twelfth attempt, when the kite came down again in exactly the same way, the smallest of them made a sound.
It was not a caw.
It was short and flat and came out of the side of its beak, and Dai understood it immediately and completely, with no evidence whatsoever, to be a criticism of his tail.

He stood in the middle of the field with the string in his hand and looked up at the wire and said, out loud, to seven birds: "It's the length on the envelope." The smallest one turned its head so that one eye was pointing at him, and said nothing at all, which was somehow much worse.
